items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The presence of caviomorph and ctenomid rodents in the Patagonian Andean Forest during the Holocene—beyond their present-day distribution, largely restricted to the steppe and steppe–forest ecotone—raises interpretive challenges. These concerns relate to the palaeoecological implications of the discrepancy between current and past distributions, as well as their potential involvement in human subsistence strategies, given the persistence of forests in this region since the Pleistocene–Holocene transition. Stable isotope analysis is a valuable approach to addressing these issues, as nitrogen isotope values in faunal and human assemblages have been shown to reflect forest resource use in Patagonia. We analysed δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C and δ
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N values in caviomorph rodent remains from the Población Anticura archaeological site, which is located within the Andean forest, around 40 km from the steppe. The assemblage includes multiple caviomorph taxa distributed across five archaeological units spanning from the Early Holocene to historical times, providing a diachronic perspective on isotopic variability. The specimens yielded mean δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C values of −22.1‰ ± 0.6‰ and δ
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N values of 2.0‰ ± 0.95‰. These results were then compared with isotopic data from steppe rodents, as well as from cervids (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Hippocamelus bisulcus</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Pudu puda</jats:italic>
                    ), which serve as ecological references for forest environments. This comparative analysis confirms an association between the Población Anticura rodents and an isotopic signal derived from the forest, highlighting the effectiveness of stable isotopes in assessing the interaction between human groups and different species in forest landscapes in northwestern Patagonia during the Holocene.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: Abstract Robust zooarchaeological analysis of Pleistocene-Holocene faunal assemblages is fundamental for reconstructing past environments, species distributions, human subsistence and faunal turnovers in North America. However, faunal remains from archaeological and palaeontological sites are commonly highly fragmented or modified, often precluding morphological identification and limiting the information they can provide about faunal communities and their relationships with human populations and changing climates. Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry (ZooMS) provides an effective biomolecular means of overcoming this limitation, enabling the identification of unidentifiable bone fragments, but its resolution depends on the availability of empirically validated reference datasets, which remain incomplete for North American fauna. Here, we expand the North American ZooMS reference library by characterizing and validating collagen peptide markers for 22 extant and extinct mammal taxa across four mammalian orders: Artiodactyla, Perissodactyla, Carnivora and Rodentia, integrating Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry fingerprinting with Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry peptide sequencing to provide sequence-level validation of diagnostic peptide markers. The resulting markers enable robust family-level discrimination across a range of taxa with genus- or species-level identification possible for several groups. This expanded reference framework enhances the taxonomic resolution and applicability of ZooMS across North American faunal assemblages, supporting its use for advancing archaeological, palaeontological and conservation-related research on the continent.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hominin and faunal fossil collections are valuable scientific resources for investigating past populations, making it critically important to preserve these rare materials and prioritise minimally destructive methods. Electron spin resonance (ESR) dating of tooth enamel typically requires laboratory irradiation of powdered subsamples; however, the effects of this treatment on organic biomolecules, and therefore their potential reuse for amino acid geochronology (AAG), remain largely unknown. This study investigates the impact of gamma irradiation on amino acids within tooth enamel, and its implications for reuse of leftover ESR-dated enamel for AAG from two palaeolithic sites: Hortus, southern France and Belle-Roche, Belgium (maximum laboratory gamma dose of 1500 and 3000 Gy respectively). Our results show that laboratory irradiation induces negligible racemisation in selected amino acids, although significant correlations between dose and D/L values emerge at higher doses (> 1200 Gy). This demonstrates that while low-level gamma irradiation (e.g. <500 Gy) does not substantially compromise the chemical integrity of amino acids in enamel, higher doses may alter racemisation patterns, potentially affecting AAG interpretation. Consequently, this supports cautious reuse of irradiated ESR powders, preferably those exposed to low laboratory doses, enabling effective reuse of finite fossil tooth enamel resources.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The Weddell Sea influences global ocean circulation and sea level through modulating Antarctic Bottom Water formation and Antarctic Ice Sheet discharges, but the history of ice‐sheet dynamics in this region remains poorly constrained due to limited well‐dated geological records. To provide a new geochemical perspective on ice‐sheet dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), this study presents paired authigenic and detrital Pb isotope records from sediment core PS1599‐3 recovered from the continental slope north of the Filchner Trough. Comparison with Antarctic Pb isotope provinces indicates that both detrital and authigenic Pb signatures were possibly sourced from a Shackleton Range‐like region in the south‐eastern Weddell Sea sector of East Antarctica. This suggests that dominant upstream drainage sources remained broadly stable throughout the last ~23 ka. We interpret the downcore Pb isotope variations to primarily reflect changes in the delivery of subglacial weathering‐derived Pb associated with grounding‐line dynamics in the Filchner Trough. Authigenic
                    <jats:sup>206</jats:sup>
                    Pb/
                    <jats:sup>204</jats:sup>
                    Pb ratios show a sharp increase at ~23 ka, followed by two decreases at ~20 and 11–9 ka. We suggest that a re‐advance of grounded ice near the LGM was followed by initial retreat at ~20 ka and further grounding‐line retreat or reorganization during the Early Holocene. These findings highlight the use of authigenic Pb isotopes as potential tracers for reconstructing polar ice‐sheet dynamics and meltwater influences.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Huang Huang, Yuanyang Hu, Marcus Gutjahr, Florian Kirsch, Lijuan Lu, Jianjun Zou, Xuefa Shi, Michael Bollen, Jimin Yu, Gerhard Kuhn

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The tongue‐bite apparatus (TBA) is a secondary jaw system found in Osteoglossomorpha and, convergently, Salmonidae. It is thought to have similar prey‐processing functions as the pharyngeal jaws, possibly allowing the oral jaws to evolve separately for more efficient prey capture. The TBA is incredibly morphologically diverse, but this diversity has not been well documented across Mormyridae, the most speciose family within Osteoglossomorpha. In this study, we examined shape diversity, levels of evolutionary integration and modularity, and rates of evolution of both the TBA and other associated components of the skull in Mormyridae, both across the family and in its two subfamilies, Petrocephalinae and Mormyrinae. Petrocephalinae, the sister group to the rest of Mormyrinae, is less species rich and has evolved independently from Mormyrinae for approximately 50 million years. This has resulted in disparity across the two groups, not only morphologically but also in terms of electric organ discharges. Results of this study support different models of modularity of the skull for these two subfamilies, with Petrocephalines having two modules as compared to Mormyrine's four modules. In both groups, the TBA makes up its own module, often evolving faster than other components of the skull. We propose that this is an example of a truly decoupled two‐jaw system, making it unique compared to the pharyngeal and oral jaws of other well‐studied groups, such as cichlids and labrids.</jats:p>
